results.summary: This design displays a bouncing Wafer.space logo with an animated color gradient on a VGA screen at 640x480 resolution. It is configured via input pins to tile the logo across the screen or to use a solid color instead of the gradient. An optional Gamepad Pmod allows starting/pausing the bounce and changing the direction or position of the logo. Silicon tests confirm it works, with testers noting that it runs at up to 32 MHz and that gamepad interaction functions correctly.

This Wokwi design sequentially displays the characters of the text "PILIPINASLASALLE" on a 7-segment display, one character per clock cycle, with the decimal point toggling each cycle. It includes a manual mode where the four BCD input pins select one of 16 predefined characters. The project is intended to be tested with a low-frequency clock (e.g., 1 Hz) and an external 7-segment display. Silicon tests show it working correctly on a demoboard.

This Wokwi project combines a simple snake game (TinySnake) with a design called PRISM, though the documentation does not describe what PRISM does. The snake game speed is controlled by the eight input pins, with larger values producing slower movement, and the game state is shown on a 7-segment display. The design requires only the on-board 7-segment display and no other external hardware. The documentation is thin and lacks details about the PRISM portion and how the two designs interact.

PVTMonitorSuite is a fully digital, modular suite for measuring gate delays, flip-flop timings, and clock skew under varying process, voltage, and temperature conditions. It uses ring oscillators and flip-flop-based measurement circuits to quantify timing characteristics, with high-speed counters converting delays into digital values. External equipment including a frequency measurement device, a precise 50 MHz signal source, and a target clock generator are required. The design avoids GF180MCU standard cells and passes all Tiny Tapeout checks.

Zedulo TestChip1 integrates UART and SPI IP blocks to convert UART data into SPI transfers and echo the SPI response back over UART. Bytes sent to the UART RX pin are transmitted out via SPI, and data received from SPI MISO is echoed on the UART TX pin. Testing requires a TTL-232 to UART interface and observing SPI activity on the SPI pins. The documentation is minimal, referring to a README that is not included.

This design implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game for VGA display, where players slide numbered tiles on a 4x4 grid to combine them and create a tile with the number 2048. The game is controlled via input pins or an optional SNES-compatible gamepad, and it includes two color themes and a unit test mode. The design requires a TinyVGA Pmod for video output and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. It supports debug commands via bidirectional pins when in unit test mode.

This is an 8-bit sequential multiply-accumulate unit designed for DSP applications, multiplying two Q0.7 fixed-point numbers and adding the result to an accumulator. It requires two 8-bit inputs, and the accumulated result is available as an 8-bit output. No external hardware has been used for testing so far. The documentation is brief and does not provide detailed usage instructions.

This is a fully functional 4-bit ALU that performs common operations such as addition, subtraction, bitwise logic, shifts, rotates, and complements on two 4-bit inputs. The operation is selected via four bidirectional pins, and a subtract mode pin determines addition or subtraction. The result appears on four output pins along with carry, zero, negative, and overflow flags. The design requires no external hardware and is tested by setting the input pins and selecting an operation.

This is an 8-bit sign-exponent-mantissa floating-point multiplier with handling for NaN and zero inputs. It multiplies two 8-bit floating-point numbers and produces an 8-bit result, and it is fully self-contained with no external hardware required. The design is purely digital and operates on a 50 MHz clock. The documentation is minimal, providing only the pinout and a brief description.

This project provides an SPI interface with two chip-select lines and four general-purpose input and output pins. The documentation is essentially absent, with "By magic" given for how it works, how to test, and what external hardware is needed. The design likely serves as a simple bridge or test chip for SPI communication, but its exact behavior cannot be determined from the provided information. The pins indicate SPI master capabilities and GPIO, but no further details are available.
